title: How I Help Schools to Teach Reading More Effectively
author: Christopher Such
summary: Such opens with a candor caveat (parts will read like a consultancy ad) and uses that to honestly map the patterns he sees across schools' reading instruction during weekly conversations with school leaders. Three recurring problems dominate: fluency development is not explicitly targeted through scaffolded reading practice; reading lessons involve precious little actual reading, especially of whole texts; and there is a lack of text discussions aimed at developing pupils' appreciation of written language and their active personal role in reading. From this Such has become convinced that teachers and leaders need to grasp the fundamentals of reading development — the connections between word recognition and the structure of the English writing system, between decoding/fluency/comprehension, and the integrated bodies of knowledge needed to make sense of a text. Schools that understand this domain make better decisions, and his consultancy work scales from hour-long keynotes through three-session sequences that introduce three lesson structures (fluency reads, extended reads, close reads), each matching one of the three priorities (build fluency through practice, read plenty of thoughtfully chosen texts, discuss texts in depth). The structures are not innovative or hard to pull off; they are tried-and-tested ways of meeting the priorities while giving teachers the support-plus-agency mix high-quality teaching needs. The closing tell: Such always provides a free or cheap alternative because he doesn't want schools spending money they don't have, and the books and free informal feedback channels are explicitly listed.
points: Three recurring problems show up in nearly every school Such advises: no explicit fluency development through scaffolded practice, very little actual reading (especially of whole texts), and no real text discussions that build pupils' appreciation and personal role in reading.

Schools that grasp the fundamentals of reading development (word recognition, English writing-system structure, decoding/fluency/comprehension links, integrated knowledge for comprehension) make better instructional decisions; lack of this foundation is what Such most consistently has to fix.

Effective reading instruction balances three priorities — build fluency through practice, read plenty of thoughtfully chosen texts, discuss texts in depth — and the three lesson structures (fluency, extended, close reads) match those one-to-one.
The lesson structures are not innovative or hard; their value is in being tried-and-tested ways of meeting the priorities while giving teachers the right mix of support and agency.

Such consistently provides free or cheap alternatives (informal feedback for state schools; his two books for the theory and practical sides) because he doesn't want schools spending money they don't have.
quotes: I have identified a number of recurring issues with schools' approaches to reading lessons, of which these are by far the most common and important: Fluency development is not explicitly targeted through scaffolded reading practice. Reading lessons involve precious little actual reading, especially of whole texts. There is a lack of text discussions aimed at developing pupils' appreciation of written language and their active, personal role in reading.

I have consistently found that schools that understand this domain make better decisions in how they approach the teaching of reading. Often I work with schools that are less confident with this domain, helping them to better understand reading so that they can develop their approach to reading with greater confidence.

If you want to support teachers to make practical changes in the classroom, sustained support is required. But when it comes to helping schools to strengthen their grasp of reading development and identify potential areas for future improvement, I'm confident that this sort of work can be useful.

Initial support on the theory behind reading is usually followed by three sessions that help schools to balance the three priorities addressed by every effective approach to teaching reading lessons: Build reading fluency through practice. Read plenty of thoughtfully chosen texts. Discuss texts in depth.

These reading lesson structures are not stunningly innovative or hugely difficult to pull off. They are also certainly not the only way to meet the three priorities of reading lessons. They are simply tried-and-tested ways of organising reading lessons that aim to meet the needs of developing readers while providing teachers with the mixture of support and agency required for high-quality teaching and ongoing improvement.

I always try to provide a free or cheap alternative to any consultancy work that I do. I do not want schools to spend money they don't have, and I don't think I could ever justify earning more than I did as a school leader.” Archived from Christopher's Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
